sections.title: Introduction
sections.text:
Welcome. Today's story reads almost like a royal drama: a beauty contest, a secret identity, an evil plot, a sleepless king, and a dramatic reversal at a banquet. It's the story of Esther, a young Jewish woman who became queen of Persia and risked her life to save her people.

The book of Esther has one surprising feature: it never once mentions the name of God. And yet, as you'll see, God's hand is at work on every page. As you listen, think about where you are in life right now, and ask: could it be that God has placed me here for a reason?

sections.title: The Story, Part 1
sections.text:
The story takes place in Shushan, the palace city of the Persian empire, during the reign of King Ahasuerus, who ruled over a hundred and twenty-seven provinces, from India to Ethiopia. After his queen, Vashti, refused to come when he called for her, the king removed her as queen and began a search for a new one.

Living in Shushan was a Jewish man named Mordecai. He had raised his young cousin, Hadassah, also called Esther, because her father and mother had died. Esther was beautiful, and she was taken to the palace along with many other young women. Mordecai told her not to reveal that she was Jewish.

Everyone who met Esther liked her. Esther chapter two, verse seventeen: “And the king loved Esther above all the women, and she obtained grace and favour in his sight more than all the virgins; so that he set the royal crown upon her head, and made her queen instead of Vashti.”

Around that time, Mordecai overheard two of the king's doorkeepers plotting to kill the king. He told Esther, Esther told the king, and the plot was stopped. It was written down in the royal records — and then seemingly forgotten.

Then the king promoted a man named Haman above all the other officials, and commanded everyone to bow to him. But Mordecai would not bow. Haman was filled with rage. And when he learned that Mordecai was a Jew, he decided it wasn't enough to punish Mordecai — he would destroy all the Jews in the whole empire. Haman cast lots, called Pur, to choose the day. Then he persuaded the king to sign a decree: on a certain day, the Jews in every province, young and old, women and children, were to be destroyed.

sections.title: The Story, Part 2
sections.text:
When Mordecai learned of the decree, he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth and ashes, and cried with a loud and bitter cry. He sent word to Esther, urging her to go to the king and plead for her people.

But there was a problem. Anyone who went to the king in the inner court without being called would be put to death — unless the king held out his golden sceptre. And the king hadn't called for Esther in thirty days.

Mordecai's reply is the heart of the book. Esther chapter four, verse fourteen: “For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, then shall there enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place; but thou and thy father's house shall be destroyed: and who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?”

Esther made her decision. She asked all the Jews in Shushan to fast for her for three days, and she and her maidens would fast too. Then she said, “and so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish.”

On the third day, Esther put on her royal robes and stood in the inner court. When the king saw her, he held out the golden sceptre. He asked, what is your request? It shall be given to you, even to half the kingdom. Wisely, Esther simply invited the king and Haman to a banquet. At the banquet, she invited them to a second banquet the next day.

Haman went home proud and happy — until he saw Mordecai at the gate, still refusing to bow. So he had a gallows built, fifty cubits high, planning to ask the king the next morning to hang Mordecai on it.

But that very night, the king could not sleep. He asked for the royal records to be read to him, and he heard how Mordecai had saved his life. He asked, what honor has been given to Mordecai for this? Nothing, his servants said. Just then Haman arrived. The king asked him, what should be done for the man the king delights to honor? Haman, thinking the king meant him, described a royal robe, the king's horse, and a parade through the city. The king said, do all of that — for Mordecai the Jew. Haman had to lead Mordecai through the streets himself.

At the second banquet, Esther finally made her plea: let my life be given me, and my people. For we are sold, to be destroyed. The king asked, who would dare do such a thing? Esther said, “The adversary and enemy is this wicked Haman.” Haman was hanged on the very gallows he had built for Mordecai. Mordecai was given Haman's position, and a new decree allowed the Jews to defend themselves. The day meant for their destruction became a day of victory. And to this day, the Jewish people celebrate that deliverance at the feast of Purim.

sections.title: The Lesson
sections.text:
What does Esther's story teach us?

First, God is at work even when we can't see Him. His name never appears in the book, yet look at the timing: a Jewish orphan becomes queen, Mordecai's good deed is recorded, and the king can't sleep on exactly the right night. Nothing is coincidence. When God seems silent in your life, He has not stopped working.

Second, you may be where you are “for such a time as this.” Esther didn't choose her position, but God placed her there for a purpose. Your job, your family, your neighborhood, your circle of friends — God may have put you there so that you can be a blessing to someone else.

Third, courage often means speaking up for others. Esther was safe in the palace, and she could have stayed quiet. Instead she risked everything for people in danger. Sometimes love requires us to use our voice.

And finally, prayer comes before action. Before Esther went to the king, she and her people fasted for three days. Big decisions deserve time spent seeking God first.

sections.title: Prayer and Reflection
sections.text:
Think about where God has placed you right now. Who might need you to speak up for them, or to show them kindness, “for such a time as this”?

Let's pray. Sovereign Lord, thank You that You are always at work, even when I can't see You. Show me why You've placed me where I am. Give me Esther's courage to speak up for others and to trust You with the outcome. In Jesus' name, Amen.

Thank you for listening. Next time, we'll move into the New Testament with the birth of Jesus.
